intro:
By the end of this track you can explain what a blocked socket read costs, and why ten thousand idle connections broke servers that give every connection its own thread. You can write a correct `java.nio` select loop, build and test Netty 4.2 pipelines with codecs, flow control and leak detection, and reason about Vert.x contexts, the event bus and the blocked-thread checker. You can predict which thread runs a Quarkus REST endpoint, set up Jetty 12's thread pool and virtual threads, and choose a server model for a service, down to what the kernel does with `epoll`, `sendfile` and io_uring. One picture runs through all eight lessons: a post office, whose clerks, walls of lit boxes, back office and loading dock stand for the threads, selectors, worker pools and kernel calls of a real server.

The track assumes no knowledge of NIO, Netty, Vert.x, Quarkus or Jetty. It builds each layer by hand first: a blocking server, then a select loop, then the same ideas in Netty, then the frameworks built on Netty and one that isn't. You need the basics from the first track (threads, locks, races), Little's law from the executors track ("Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law"), and the virtual threads track, which this one connects back to in lessons 1, 6, 7 and 8. Versions are pinned: JDK 21 or newer (install JDK 25, the current long-term support release), Netty 4.2.20.Final, Vert.x 5.2.3, Quarkus 3.40 and Jetty 12.1.14.

The labs live in `labs/nio`, one package per lesson (`workbench.nio.l01` to `l08`). Lessons 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 have Java labs; lessons 3, 6 and 8 are in Kotlin. Run `./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.lNN.*'` from `labs/` until it passes, and `./gradlew :nio:solutionTest` to check the reference answers. Servers in the tests bind `127.0.0.1` on a free port, so nothing clashes with what you have running. The Try-it demos run with `./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=...`, in Java and Kotlin. A few steps use Linux tools (`strace`, `epoll`, io_uring); on macOS the same demos run on `kqueue` and say so.
cheatsheet:
## The post office, lesson by lesson

| Lesson | The idea | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A blocked read holds its thread; thread-per-connection needs a thread per open socket (C10K) | a clerk for each customer, waiting at the counter while they fill in a form; 10,000 customers need 10,000 clerks |
| 2 | A `Selector` tells one thread which channels are ready; reads and writes move only what fits | one clerk watching a wall of boxes with lights; a `ByteBuffer` is a tray with a cursor and a stop line |
| 2 | Linux selectors are level-triggered; `OP_WRITE` left on spins | a light that stays on while there's mail; the "room for a reply" light that never goes out |
| 3 | An event loop owns its channels for life; a pipeline of handlers; never block the loop | a clerk who owns a row of boxes, an in-tray for notes from other threads, a line of stations, and a clerk who never stops to make a phone call |
| 3 | Offload blocking work to your own executor, write the reply from there | the back office |
| 4 | Frame, decode, release every `ByteBuf`, watch writability | the page count on the envelope; trays from a shared stack; the night inspector; a full out-tray with two painted marks |
| 5 | Vert.x contexts, verticles, the event bus, `executeBlocking` | desks served by one clerk each, mail tubes between desks, a floor manager who only takes notes, a back office that works in single file unless told otherwise |
| 6 | Quarkus picks the thread from the signature | a rule book that reads only the label on each job: counter clerk, back office or temporary helper |
| 7 | Jetty's acceptors, selectors and adaptive strategy | doormen, light-watchers who serve quick jobs themselves, standby clerks, one staff room |
| 8 | Zero-copy, epoll and io_uring, the JDK's poller | the loading dock that skips the counter; a board of lit boxes; a drop box for a whole list of jobs; the JDK's own light-watcher |

## Numbers worth remembering

| What | Default or rule |
|---|---|
| Threads a blocking design needs | Little's law: in flight = rate × time; thread-per-connection needs one per open socket |
| Netty event loops | 2 × CPUs |
| Netty water marks | low 32 KiB, high 64 KiB (`isWritable()` flips between them) |
| Netty leak detection | SIMPLE samples about 1 in 128 buffers; use PARANOID in tests |
| Vert.x event loops / worker pool | 2 × CPUs / 20 threads |
| Vert.x blocked-thread checker | checks every 1 s; warns past 2 s; stack trace past 5 s |
| Vert.x event bus request timeout | 30 s |
| Quarkus event loops | `max(2, min(maxHeapMB / 10, CPUs))`; warning and stack trace at 2 s |
| Quarkus blocking executor | `quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads` = max(8 × CPUs, 200) |
| Jetty `QueuedThreadPool` | min 8, max 200, queue must stay unbounded |
| Jetty connector | 1 acceptor; `max(1, min(CPUs / 2, maxThreads / 16))` selectors |
| Tomcat NIO connector | `maxThreads` 200, `maxConnections` 8192, `acceptCount` 100 |
| JDK poller on Linux | JDK 21: `Read-Poller` / `Write-Poller` platform threads; JDK 22+: `MasterPoller` + one virtual read sub-poller per core (power of 2, at most 32) |

## The select loop rules (lesson 2)

- `flip()` before reading a buffer, `compact()` after a partial write, never `clear()` with bytes pending.
- One `read` is not one message: frame with a length or a delimiter.
- Remove every handled key from `selectedKeys()`.
- `OP_WRITE` only while bytes are pending; drop `OP_READ` while your buffer is full; close on EOF only when drained.

## Netty 4.2: group, pipeline, offload (lessons 3 and 4)

```java
EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory());   // not NioEventLoopGroup
new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class)
        .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
            @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) {
                ch.pipeline().addLast(new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4),   // the page count
                        new LetterFrameDecoder(), new LetterFrameEncoder(), new LetterHandler(backOffice));
            }
        }).bind(9000).sync();

// in your LetterHandler.channelRead0: never block the loop
backOffice.execute(() -> ctx.writeAndFlush(priceBook.reply(letter)));   // writeAndFlush is safe from any thread
```

```kotlin
val group = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory())                  // not NioEventLoopGroup
ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java)
    .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
        override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) {
            ch.pipeline().addLast(LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4),   // the page count
                LetterFrameDecoder(), LetterFrameEncoder(), LetterHandler(backOffice))
        }
    }).bind(9000).sync()

// in your LetterHandler.channelRead0: never block the loop
backOffice.execute { ctx.writeAndFlush(priceBook.reply(letter)) }            // writeAndFlush is safe from any thread
```

`LetterFrameDecoder` and `LetterFrameEncoder` are lesson 4's lab classes, which `LetterCodec.handlers(business)` puts in this order. Release rule: whoever touches a `ByteBuf` last releases it. `fireChannelRead` and `write` hand ownership on, as `CountingTap` does; `SimpleChannelInboundHandler` releases after `channelRead0`. Backpressure: in `channelReadComplete`, `if (!isWritable) autoRead = false`; in `channelWritabilityChanged`, turn it back on. Close with `writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE)`.

## Vert.x 5: deploy desks, offload without single file (lesson 5)

```java
vertx.deployVerticle(PriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));
vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(parcel), false)   // false: calls from one context may overlap
        .onSuccess(msg::reply);
```

```kotlin
vertx.deployVerticle(::PriceDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))   // a bare lambda is ambiguous in Kotlin
vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(parcel) }, false)   // false: calls may overlap
    .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) }
```

## Quarkus REST 3.40: which thread? (lesson 6)

| Endpoint | Thread | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| returns a plain value | worker (executor) | the back office |
| returns `Uni`, `Multi`, `CompletionStage`, `Publisher`, or is Kotlin `suspend` | IO thread (event loop) | a job labeled "quick" stays with the counter clerk |
| `@Blocking` / `@NonBlocking` | worker / IO thread, overriding the signature | a new label on the ticket |
| `@Transactional` | blocking per the 3.40.1 docs, not per main: add `@Blocking` | the rule book that argues with itself |
| `@RunOnVirtualThread` | a new virtual thread | a temporary helper for one job |

## Jetty 12: honest handlers, virtual threads for blocking work (lesson 7)

```java
QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(200);
pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-"));
// Handler.Abstract = BLOCKING: EPC or PEC (virtual thread). Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking = runs on the selector (PC).
```

```kotlin
val pool = QueuedThreadPool(200)
pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-")
// Handler.Abstract = BLOCKING: EPC or PEC (virtual thread). Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking = runs on the selector (PC).
```

## Zero-copy and the kernel (lesson 8)

```java
long sent = 0;
while (sent < count) sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket);   // sendfile on Linux
```

```kotlin
var sent = 0L
while (sent < count) sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket)   // sendfile on Linux
```

No zero-copy when the JVM must change the bytes (TLS in the JVM, compression). `epoll` = readiness, io_uring = completion; measure before switching. A virtual thread's blocking read = non-blocking read + JDK `Poller` (epoll one-shot) + park.

## Choosing a model

| Service | Model | Limit lives in | Picture it |
|---|---|---|---|
| blocking code (database calls, blocking libraries), mostly waiting | virtual threads per request | a semaphore or pool per downstream | temporary helpers, with a fixed number of tickets for the database counter |
| blocking code, moderate traffic | bounded worker pool | the pool size (Little's law) | a back office with a fixed staff |
| non-blocking end to end | event loop (Netty, Vert.x, Quarkus `Uni`) | never waiting; writability and auto-read | one clerk per row of boxes, never on the phone |
| many idle long-lived connections | event loop | memory per connection, idle timeouts | a wall of dark boxes and a few clerks |
| large unchanged files | `transferTo` / `DefaultFileRegion` | the socket buffer (loop on partial transfers) | the loading dock |
recap: A blocked read holds its thread, so thread-per-connection needs one thread per open socket, which is why ten thousand idle connections (C10K) broke it. Little's law sizes the threads a blocking design needs.

A `java.nio` server reads and writes partially: keep unsent bytes, `compact()` instead of `clear()`, remove selected keys, and arm `OP_WRITE` only while bytes are pending, because Linux selectors are level-triggered.

A Netty event loop is one thread that owns its channels for life. Netty 4.2 builds groups with `MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup` and an `IoHandler` factory, and you dispatch blocking work to your own executor by hand.
Frame before you decode, release every `ByteBuf` exactly once (the last owner releases), catch leaks with PARANOID detection in tests, and turn auto-read off while a channel isn't writable.

Vert.x puts contexts on Netty's loops: a handler never runs at the same time as itself, the event bus is best effort, the blocked-thread checker only reports after 2 s, and `executeBlocking` is ordered per context unless you pass `false`.

Quarkus REST picks the thread from the signature: reactive types and `suspend` run on the IO thread, plain values on a worker. Add `@Blocking` to JTA endpoints that return `Uni`, and use `@RunOnVirtualThread` with explicit limits in front of every downstream.

Jetty 12 decides per task from the handler's declared invocation type: non-blocking on the selector thread, blocking with a reserved thread taking over or handed off, optionally to virtual threads. Its pool queue must stay unbounded.
Virtual threads hide an event loop inside the JDK's poller. Zero-copy (`sendfile`) and io_uring are kernel tools to measure, and every server model still needs a concurrency limit somewhere.

quiz.q: A thread-per-connection server keeps 6,000 parcel lockers connected. They send 300 requests a second in total, each taking 100 ms. How many threads does the server hold?
options: About 6,000
One per CPU core
quiz.why: Little's law gives 300 × 0.1 s = 30 requests in flight, but thread-per-connection keeps a thread on every open socket, busy or idle: about 6,000. That gap is the C10K problem in miniature.

quiz.q: An NIO server burns one core at 100% with no traffic. Which change fixes it?
options: Use direct buffers instead of heap buffers
Register `OP_WRITE` only while a connection has unsent bytes
Call `selectNow()` instead of `select()`
Add a second selector thread
quiz.why: A socket with free send-buffer space is always writable, and Linux selectors are level-triggered, so a permanent `OP_WRITE` makes every `select()` return at once: the light that never goes out. `selectNow()` would spin even harder.

quiz.q: In Netty 4.2, a handler must call a library that looks prices up in a slow database the blocking way. What is the recommended way?
options: `pipeline.addLast(new DefaultEventExecutorGroup(8), "prices", handler)`
Call it in the handler; Netty 4.2 loops are virtual threads
Dispatch the call to your own executor and `ctx.writeAndFlush` the result from there
Wrap the call in `synchronized`
quiz.why: Netty 4.2 deprecated the per-handler `EventExecutorGroup` versions of `addLast` and says to dispatch by hand. Event loops are platform threads, and `writeAndFlush` from another thread is queued back onto the channel's loop.

quiz.q: A Netty handler extends `ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter`, logs `msg.readableBytes()`, and then does nothing else with the `ByteBuf`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the garbage collector frees it
It leaks: it neither passes the buffer on nor releases it
It releases the buffer twice
It blocks the event loop
quiz.why: `ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter` releases nothing. A handler that is the last to touch a buffer must release it (`ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg)`) or pass it on with `ctx.fireChannelRead(msg)`, as lesson 4's `CountingTap` does. PARANOID leak detection reports it once the buffer is garbage-collected.

quiz.q: A Netty relay forwards from a fast client to a slow central server. The central channel's `isWritable()` turns false. What should the relay do?
options: Turn off auto-read on the client channel until the central channel is writable again
Keep writing; Netty buffers it
Close the central channel
Sleep in the handler until the central server catches up
quiz.why: Writability is Netty's signal that the outbound buffer passed the high water mark. Stopping reads from the producer keeps the backlog in the kernel and TCP, not in your memory; sleeping would block the event loop.

quiz.q: A Vert.x consumer wraps a 300 ms database call in `vertx.executeBlocking(callable)`. Six requests arrive at once. Roughly how long until all six are answered?
options: About 300 ms
About 600 ms
About 1,800 ms, because executeBlocking is ordered per context by default
Never: it deadlocks
quiz.why: All six messages come from the consumer's one context, and the default `executeBlocking` runs calls from a context one after another. The event loop is free, but the calls wait in single file. Pass `false` to let them overlap.

quiz.q: In Quarkus 3.40, which endpoint blocks an IO thread?
options: `public Price get(...)` that calls a database the blocking way
`@Blocking public Uni<Price> get(...)` that calls a database the blocking way
`@RunOnVirtualThread public Price get(...)` that calls a database the blocking way
`public Uni<Price> get(...)` that returns `Uni.createFrom().item(db.find(id))`
quiz.why: A `Uni` return type puts the method on the IO thread, and `db.find(id)` runs while the `Uni` is being built. The other three run on a worker or a virtual thread.

quiz.q: A Jetty 12 health-check handler extends `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking`, and someone adds a database ping to it. What happens under load?
options: Jetty notices and moves it to a worker thread
It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each ping
It runs on a virtual thread
Jetty rejects the handler at startup
quiz.why: `NonBlocking` is a promise Jetty trusts: it runs the handler directly on the selector thread. Blocking there stalls the selector, which Jetty's docs call a risk of server lock-up. Change the superclass to `Handler.Abstract`.

quiz.q: On JDK 21, what happens when a virtual thread calls `socket.getInputStream().read()` and no data has arrived?
options: Its carrier thread blocks in the kernel until data arrives
The JVM creates a new platform thread for the read
The read throws, and the virtual thread retries in a loop
The JDK does a non-blocking read, registers the socket with its internal poller and parks the virtual thread; a poller thread unparks it when data arrives
quiz.why: `NioSocketImpl` keeps the socket non-blocking, gets EAGAIN, registers the file descriptor with the `Poller` (epoll, one-shot) and parks. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads such as `Read-Poller`; from JDK 22 on Linux, one platform `MasterPoller` drives virtual sub-pollers.

quiz.q: A service sends 500 MB logbook files to an internal archive over a plain TCP link. Which code sends them most efficiently, and what must it handle?
options: A loop of `FileChannel.transferTo` calls, because a call may transfer fewer bytes than asked
`Files.readAllBytes` then one `write`; nothing else
Netty with io_uring, because it is always fastest
A heap `ByteBuffer` of 500 MB
quiz.why: `transferTo` to a socket becomes `sendfile` on Linux, so the bytes never pass through the JVM, and it can return early, so it belongs in a loop. Reading 500 MB into the heap wastes memory, and io_uring was not faster in this track's runs.
